newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin tempers single currency enthusiasm.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin tempers single currency enthusiasm.

text.p: Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin, the head of the main opposition party, tempered his support for a European single currency on Sunday when he said that, if elected, he would not introduce further austerity measures to ensure France meets strict targets to join monetary union, scheduled for 1999.
Speculation mounted in France on Sunday that President Jacques Chirac would announce a snap general election on Monday to clear the decks in the drive for a single European currency.

Jospin said in a television interview that he was against further economic austerity as France was already facing record unemployment and that he would not say yes, unconditionally, to monetary union if that were to lead to even longer jobless queues.

Jospin said, "If to respect the criteria of three percent, which Germany will probably not respect, if to do that we have to impose, with the jobless rate we have...a new cure of austerity on the country my answer is no. No to the absolute respect of the three percent criterion," he said.

Amid growing doubts about France's ability to reduce its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said last week the government would take all measures necessary to meet its goal.

Socialist support for the single currency has so far prevented an electoral pact with the anti-Maastricht Communists, but Jospin said if his conditions for joining a single currency were met the Communist Party should also change its stance.

"Is there a problem with the Communists? It's not Europe in general, it's the euro. I say it is a yes. Yes if the conditions are met...The Communists say no, but I say if the conditions are met it is their responsibility to say yes."

Jospin said if European nations chose to enter a single currency they would do so for political reasons, or as part of a historic vision, not for reasons of petty accounting related to the entry criteria.
"I propose that we open discussions with our partners to know under what conditions we will go ahead with the euro...We will have one year to relaunch a real dialogue with Germany."
In outlining his policy towards monetary union, Jospin said both Italy and Spain should take part in a single currency from the start.
Speculation was rife last week that France and Germany were planning a deal to exclude Italy and Spain from the first wave of participants, despite denials from Paris and Bonn.

Jospin also weighed into the debate about whether a future independent European central banks should be subject to checks from a European political body. He said there should be, what he dubbed, an "economic government" opposite the central bank.

France's call for a special council to co-ordinate economic policy inside monetary union was won grudging acceptance from other European states recently, although it is now only likely to be an informal forum.
